terms.grammar: interjection; anywhere in the clause, often after its first word
terms.register: vōx cōmica et sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.
evidence: Ter. Ph. 386: Periī hercle: nōmen perdidī.
terms.comment: The vocative of Herculēs. A man’s oath.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 2.5.2: sed mehercule nē, cum vēneris, nōn habeās jam quod cūrēs
terms.comment: The form of Cicero’s letters, where hercle is rare.

terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; pol also Hor.
evidence: Plaut. Most. 376: Quaesō edepol, exsurge; pater advenit.
Traupman p. 98: eu edepol, eu hercle, geez
terms.comment: Said by men and women alike (Gellius).

evidence: Plaut. Amph. 508: Ēcastor tē experior quantī faciās uxōrem tuam.

terms.gloss: so help me God! as true as heaven!
terms.register: Cic. in epistulīs; Sall., Plin. Ep.
evidence: Cic. Fam. 5.21.1: ūnum medius fidius tēcum diem libentius posuerim
terms.comment: Lewis & Short (s.v. Fidius): an oath by the god of good faith, “as true as heaven!”; also written as one word.

phrases.latin: Quid agis, mea salūs? — Ēsuriō hercle, atque adeō hau salūbriter.
phrases.english: How are you, my darling? — Starving, by Hercules, and not in a healthy way.
Heavens, I’m done for: I’ve forgotten the name.

phrases.latin: sed mehercule nē, cum vēneris, nōn habeās jam quod cūrēs
phrases.english: but, honestly, I fear that when you come you’ll have nothing left to look after

phrases.latin: Mē ad cēnam vocā. — Pol vērō vocō.
phrases.english: Invite me to dinner. — I do indeed invite you.

phrases.latin: Ēcastor tē experior quantī faciās uxōrem tuam.
phrases.english: Truly, I find out how much you value your wife.

phrases.latin: ūnum medius fidius tēcum diem libentius posuerim quam hoc omne tempus cum plērīsque eōrum, quibuscum vīvō necessāriō
phrases.english: so help me, I would rather spend one day with you than all this time with most of those I have to live with

gellius.html: Gell. 11.6.1 (and Charisius): in the old writers Roman women do not swear by Hercules, nor men by Castor; edepol is common to both. Lewis & Short (s.v. Castor) finds ēcastor “especially by women, though not exclusively by them”. The plays bear the rule out on the whole (loci-plautus).
